#219426. Latest Update: For decades, scientists may have misunderstood how brain cells work

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1262 w)

Latest Update: For decades, scientists may have misunderstood how brain cells work

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1262 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even before a new neuroscience study appeared in Nature, its preliminary version had been downloaded more than 11,000 times.
  • In a recent development, do neurons operate like individual tools, such as hammers and saws, each designed for a particular job?
  • Researchers at Columbia's Zuckerman Institute examined an extensive collection of mouse brain recordings gathered through an international collaboration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even before a new neuroscience study appeared in Nature, its preliminary version had been downloaded more than 11,000 times. The research addresses one of the oldest and most hotly debated questions in neuroscience: how specialized are the individual cells that make up the brain?

In a recent development, do neurons operate like individual tools, such as hammers and saws, each designed for a particular job? Or are they more like Swiss Army knives, capable of handling many different tasks?

Researchers at Columbia's Zuckerman Institute examined an extensive collection of mouse brain recordings gathered through an international collaboration. Their analysis revealed that while some neurons are indeed specialists, most appear capable of responding to many different kinds of information.

Sources indicate that "We have to move away from this image of the brain as a machine made of gears, with every gear having an exact purpose that we can attach a label to," noted Stefano Fusi, PhD, a principal investigator at Columbia's Zuckerman Institute, a member of the Kavli Institute for Brain Science and the paper's co-senior author. "The brain doesn't work like that. Instead, most neurons can display a huge diversity of responses, and this can help the brain solve a huge number of different tasks.".

Sources indicate that the discovery could help explain how the brain achieves its remarkable ability to perform complex tasks. It could also provide a foundation for understanding what happens when brain function is disrupted and identifying ways to restore it.

Revisiting a Decades-Old Neuroscience Debate.

According to recent reports, the question of whether neurons are specialists or generalists "is an old, important question, and one which researchers have really strong opinions on," noted Lorenzo Posani, PhD, the study's co-lead author and a principal investigator at the Paris Brain Institute and France's CNRS. Posani conducted the research while working at Columbia's Zuckerman Institute.

Recent findings suggest that scientists have long known that the brain contains distinct regions responsible for functions such as sight and smell. This organization suggests that individual neurons might also have narrowly defined roles. However, the brain is also an extraordinarily powerful biological computer capable of adapting to countless situations, raising the possibility that its individual neurons are similarly versatile.

One reason the debate has persisted is that researchers have approached the question under widely different experimental conditions, Posani explained. Previous studies examined different animal species, investigated different parts of the brain, or required animals to complete different activities. Unsurprisingly, their conclusions often conflicted. Some experiments identified highly specialized neurons, while others revealed cells with much broader capabilities.

A Massive Study of 43 Brain Regions.

To obtain a more consistent picture of neural activity, the researchers focused exclusively on mice performing the same type of task. They also examined numerous brain regions simultaneously, drawing on datasets considerably larger than those typically used in neuroscience research.

The recordings, collected by the International Brain Laboratory consortium, captured the activity of individual neurons across 43 regions of the mouse cerebral cortex.

The analysis revealed an crucial distinction. Neurons in primary sensory regions, including areas responsible for processing visual information, tended to exhibit more specialized responses. Across other regions, however, individual neurons displayed a considerably wider range of activity. The overall findings suggest that generalists, rather than specialists, dominate much of the cortex.

"We're not saying that there are no specialized neurons," noted Dr. Fusi, who is also a professor of neuroscience at Columbia's Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons and a member of Columbia's Center for Theoretical Neuroscience. "We're saying they are the exceptions. They're not the rule.".

Most Neurons Are Versatile in Different Ways.

Despite the versatility of individual neurons, the brain retains a distinct regional organization. By examining how a neuron responded during a particular task, the scientists could identify with surprising accuracy which functional module it belonged to. Yet membership in a particular brain module did not generally mean that a neuron was limited to a single function.

Industry observers note that "For example, compare this to maps of voter opinions," Dr. Posani mentioned. "There are clear clusters where people generally vote the same way. But when you zoom in, you see mixes of opinions.".

Sources indicate that the researchers also uncovered another striking feature of neural activity. Not only do most neurons handle multiple kinds of information, but their patterns of activity rarely mirror those of other neurons.

According to recent reports, "Each is versatile in its own way," claims study co-lead author Shuqi Wang, a doctoral student at École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne in Switzerland. According to Wang, this diversity helps give the brain its flexibility and impressive computational abilities.

The Secret Behind the Brain's Computing Power.

The researchers propose that the versatility of neurons allows individual brain cells to represent several types of information at once. For example, a neuron might respond to both the color of an object, such as red or black, and its shape, such as a circle or square.

Recent findings suggest that working together, groups of neurons can form what scientists call "high-dimensional" representations of information. These representations capture multiple characteristics simultaneously, allowing the brain to distinguish a red circle from a black square, for instance.

This arrangement gives groups of neurons considerable flexibility in how they process incoming information and generate responses. Rather than requiring an entirely separate neural representation for every new task, the brain can draw on existing combinations of neural activity.

In a recent development, "You can reuse these high-dimensional representations for lots of different tasks," Dr. Fusi remarked.

Rethinking How Scientists Study the Brain.

The findings also have significant implications for how neuroscientists investigate brain function. Because a single neuron can carry information about several different variables, determining precisely what it represents by examining its activity alone can be extremely difficult.

A clearer picture emerges when scientists analyze the combined activity of many neurons, much as the brain itself processes information through populations of cells.

It has been revealed that this represents an vital change in perspective for the neuroscience community, "which for decades focused on one neuron at a time, discarding all neurons whose responses could not be understood," Dr. Fusi mentioned.

Do Human Brain Cells Work the Same Way?

The researchers are now collaborating with Ueli Rutishauser's research group at Caltech to determine whether human neurons exhibit similar patterns of versatility.

They also hope to establish whether the degree of specialization among neurons changes depending on the particular demands of a task.

Recent findings suggest that "There is still a lot to discover," Dr. Fusi noted.

The paper, "Rarely categorical and highly separable: how neural representations change along the cortical hierarchy," was published in Nature.

The full list of authors includes Lorenzo Posani, Shuqi Wang, Samuel P. Muscinelli, Liam Paninski and Stefano Fusi.

In a recent development, the research received funding from the National Institutes of Health (RF1AG080818, U19NS123716), the Simons Foundation, the Kavli Foundation, the Gatsby Foundation (GAT3708), and the Swartz Foundation. Additional support was provided by the National Science Foundation and the DoD Office of the Under Secretary of Defense (R&E) under Cooperative Agreement PHY-2229929 (the NSF AI Institute for Artificial and Natural Intelligence). Dr. Posani received additional support through the NIH 1K99MH135166-01 grant.

Sources indicate that materials provided by The Zuckerman Institute at Columbia University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that with Black Friday finally here, Pokémon fans can get their hands on some of the year's most popular trading card releases for considerably less. There are plenty of worthwhile discounts to grab before this huge shopping event comes to a close.

According to recent reports, the sale carries on across the whole weekend, and we've rounded up the best Pokémon deals at the moment available across Amazon and other retailers, covering everything from Elite Trainer Boxes and Booster Bundles to Lego sets and Nintendo Switch games. We'll continue updating this guide as more bargains go live ahead of Cyber Monday, so be sure to keep checking back for the latest price cuts.

Industry observers note that for a while, this Pokémon TCG 30th Celebration Elite Trainer Box was only available via "request invite" at Amazon, then it disappeared. It's available at Walmart, where it's been marked down for Black Friday to market price at just $115.96. Walmart usually lists this one at a very pricey $237.98, so it's a huge markdown — but only while supplies last. The Pokémon deals are going fast, so it's entirely possible this one will disappear again.

Recent findings suggest that stocks of this booster bundle have held firm, but we can see them being snapped up by deal-hungry collectors. With a discount of over $20, it's a great price for this box of six booster packs. You get 60 game cards in total, with powerful Mega Pokémon like Darkrai ex and Zeraora ex to find. This set is also a great jumping-off point for Chaos Rising.

If you don’t feel like paying three figures for a display box or waiting for an ETB invite, you can still buy into Pokémon’s 30th Celebration expansion with the Tech Sticker Collection — now under $35 at Walmart.

Recent findings suggest that in this particular collection, you get three boosters, a Lucario or Alolan Exeggutor foil promo, and a matching sticker sheet. Plus, our own pricing research has shown this is close to another all-time low from third-party sellers.

If you’re a Pokémon TCG collector who’s hoping to catch up on the Delta Reign expansion with more packs for less this Black Friday, the price for this huge 36-pack Booster Display Box has been knocked down to $199.99 at Amazon from its current standard $223.99 list price — for a $24 saving, working out to $5.55 per booster pack.

Sources indicate that that’s only $5.10 above its current TCGplayer market price of $194.89. In the expansion as a whole, there are over 140 cards to collect, including Mega Rayquaza ex and Mega Golurk ex, so there are plenty of potential pulls to chase.

Topics Black Friday Gaming Pokemon Trading Cards.

If you spot a solid discount on a Pokémon TCG pack, box, or collection you haven’t seen before (like a 30th Celebration ETB, Delta Reign Booster Bundle, etc.), it’s worth buying now rather than waiting for Black Friday.

It has been revealed that when you see a particular price drop, that deal is more likely specific to one or several sellers than to the industry market price across all sellers — depending on their own stock allocations. When that stock is gone, it’s uncertain whether those sellers will have any more units coming in, or even at the same lower price point.

Although more Pokémon cards are being printed than ever in 2026, the Pokémon TCG still has the same glitch that sees any readily available selection of packs, or boxes of packs, being sold for above MSRP: There is nowhere near enough supply to meet the demand.

As a result, prices for readily available cards are dictated by market price: estimated by factors like pull rates, the most valuable cards in an expansion, how many print runs an expansion has had, and their overall contribution to the meta.

It has been revealed that day-to-day deals vary between standard Pokémon TCG retailers like Amazon, Walmart, and Target — but the best Black Friday deals are likely to be from third-party sellers operating through those storefronts. There are a lot of sellers competing for sales with one another to offload their stock, and Black Friday is still the ideal season to undercut other Pokémon TCG merchants. Keep checking this guide and store listings each day for the best newly revealed deals.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Discounts on already budget-oriented laptops are often sparse.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that thanksgiving is over, and the Black Friday laptop deals are rolling in. As WIRED’s head laptop reviewer, I’m seeing solid discounts on some of the best laptops I’ve tested this year, whether you’re looking for a new MacBook, Windows laptop, or gaming device.

Want more deals? Check out our guide to the Best Black Friday Deals, the Best Black Friday TV Deals, and the Best Tech Deals.

Discounts on already budget-oriented laptops are often sparse. That’s been true for the Dell XPS 13 ever since it relaunched a few months ago, holding steady at a starting price of either $700 or $750. But for Black Friday, Dell’s dropped the price by $200 to just $550. It’s astounding that you can get a laptop of this caliber for that price, especially given how premium it feels. The chassis is well-built and highly portable; the display is both bright and colorful, and the trackpad feels great to use. However, this $550 model comes with only 8 GB of RAM, which might be a sticking point for many people. You can upgrade to 16 GB, but it’s not on sale for Black Friday.

Back in June, Apple raised the price of the MacBook Air to $1,299. It felt inevitable, but as a laptop reviewer, it still crushed my spirits. The M5 MacBook Air is the laptop most people should buy, but at $1,299, I knew it was a stretch for most budgets. That’s what makes this Amazon discount feel so impactful. It brings the MacBook Air down to $1,049, making it the first time it’s been close to its original price since June.

Industry observers note that the MacBook Neo is already cheap, so Apple has no incentive to cut the price—even though the laptop has been out for seven months. But finally, the MacBook Neo’s price has dropped by $50, bringing it down to $649. That’s a great deal, especially if you’re looking for an affordable laptop that feels premium, with a metal chassis and quality display. The 8 GB of RAM is limiting, but if your needs aren’t overly heavy, the MacBook Neo should do the trick—especially at this price.

According to recent reports, these days, you’ll be hard-pressed to find a laptop under $1,000 without major compromises. That’s even more uncommon for a laptop with a larger screen. But the IdeaPad Slim 5x is just that. It’s a 15-inch laptop with great performance, long-lasting battery life, lots of ports, a solid trackpad, and a high-resolution OLED screen. It even comes packed to the brim with 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage. It’s not as thin as the 15-inch MacBook Air, but it’s hundreds of dollars cheaper.

Sources indicate that it might be well over two years old, but I still recommend the 2024 Surface Laptop. The price is down to $900 right now, which is a good deal for these specs, performance, and battery life. You’re limited to the blue color option (also known as Sapphire), but it’s the best price I’ve seen on this laptop so far this year. My favorite feature will always be the 3:2 aspect ratio screen, which gives the display a taller shape for more vertical space to work with.

There is a newer version that uses the Snapdragon X2 Plus/Elite chips, but I find it quite expensive. The IdeaPad Slim 5x listed above is the better option if you’re OK with a larger device, since it uses those next-generation Snapdragon chips and twice the storage. But if you’re sold on the Surface Laptop's more premium design, this is the one to get.

With the MacBook Neo selling for $600, you might look at something like the HP OmniBook 5 with suspicion. Even on sale for $700, being $100 more than the MacBook Neo doesn’t seem like a great position for an entry-level Windows laptop. And while this laptop is often on sale, this is $100 cheaper than I’ve seen it over the past few weeks.

According to recent reports, but the HP OmniBook 5 is a special device, with its OLED display, very thin chassis, and 16 GB of RAM. It very much looks like a laptop that should cost hundreds more. Battery life is great, too, thanks to the Snapdragon X chip inside. The 16 GB of RAM is still the main selling point here—if it was any less, I would recommend the XPS 13 in nearly every scenario (but it’s not on sale right now). It’s only real downfall is the touchpad. It feels frustratingly clumsy to use, making precise movements difficult.

#219416. The surprising reason women seem better at multitasking than men

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (722 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

The surprising reason women seem better at multitasking than men

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (722 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that men and women appear to be similarly skilled at juggling multiple activities, but latest research has uncovered one striking difference.
  • It has been revealed that whether driving, working, doing household chores, or enjoying leisure activities, people frequently find themselves managing several tasks at once or switching between them.
  • With support from the Bial Foundation, researchers André and Diana Szameitat (from Brunel University of London and City St George's, University of London, UK, respectively) set out to determine whether meaningful differences exist in multitasking ability and what might explain the widespread belief that women have an advantage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that men and women appear to be similarly skilled at juggling multiple activities, but latest research has uncovered one striking difference. In an experiment designed to recreate the demands of everyday life, men ignored conversational questions more than twice as often as women while performing just as well on the other tasks.

It has been revealed that whether driving, working, doing household chores, or enjoying leisure activities, people frequently find themselves managing several tasks at once or switching between them. Although women are widely believed to be better at multitasking than men, previous research has found only minor and inconsistent differences between the sexes, raising doubts about the accuracy of this popular assumption.

With support from the Bial Foundation, researchers André and Diana Szameitat (from Brunel University of London and City St George's, University of London, UK, respectively) set out to determine whether meaningful differences exist in multitasking ability and what might explain the widespread belief that women have an advantage.

Putting Multitasking Skills to the Test.

In their study, "Men Talk Less Than Women During Multitasking," published in the scientific journal Psychological Research, the researchers developed an experiment involving five different activities. The setup was designed to capture the complexity of everyday multitasking more accurately than most previous studies.

The first experiment involved 41 men and 37 women. Participants were asked to follow a recipe in a kitchen setting, look up phone numbers, match numbers with letters, watch a slideshow for specific words, and answer conversational questions. A fresh question was posed every 20 seconds (e.g., "Would you rather lose all of your money and valuables or all of the pictures you have ever taken, and why?").

In a second experiment, the researchers recruited 160 observers to determine whether differences in multitasking behavior were noticeable to others. Without being given prior information about the participants or findings, the observers watched video recordings of the experiments and assessed how well the participants performed.

One Surprising Difference Between Men and Women.

Men and women achieved comparable results on four of the five activities. Conversation, however, revealed a notable exception. Men left conversational questions unanswered more than twice as often as women. When men did answer, their responses were just as fast and of comparable quality to those given by women.

Industry observers note that the researchers suggest that women may, on average, be more inclined to engage in communication during social interactions. However, the study did not directly investigate this possibility, so the explanation should be treated with caution. The results are also consistent with evolutionary theories suggesting that women may have a greater tendency to engage in conversation.

How Conversation Shapes Perceptions of Ability.

The differences in conversational engagement appeared to have a considerable impact on how others judged the participants. Observers rated men as having less control over the activities, performing more poorly, putting in less effort, and being less alert than women. They also perceived men as less happy and as deriving less enjoyment from the experience.

Rather than revealing a broad difference in multitasking ability between men and women, the research points to a much more specific behavioral distinction: men are more likely to leave conversations unanswered when managing several activities simultaneously.

Because conversational engagement is easily noticed by others, this difference may create the impression that men are less effective at multitasking, even when their performance on other activities is comparable to that of women. The findings offer a potential explanation for how the popular stereotype that women are better multitaskers developed and why it continues to persist.

"Taken together, our data confirm that there are no substantial sex differences in cognitive visual-manual tasks, but that significant sex differences do exist in the ability to hold a conversation while multitasking," explains André Szameitat. This is "an ability highly salient in everyday life and, thus, could explain the development of the widespread public stereotype that women are better at multitasking than men," the researcher concludes.

  • Once-struggling retailers are entering the holiday quarter with improved performance and sales momentum as turnaround efforts begin to resonate with shoppers.
  • A handful of earnings reports on Tuesday pointed to a mix of factors behind the strong results, including a resilient consumer, stronger execution and demand for the right products at the right price.
  • Kohl's reported comparable sales growth of 1.2% for the period ended Oct.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Once-struggling retailers are entering the holiday quarter with improved performance and sales momentum as turnaround efforts begin to resonate with shoppers.

A handful of earnings reports on Tuesday pointed to a mix of factors behind the strong results, including a resilient consumer, stronger execution and demand for the right products at the right price.

Kohl's reported comparable sales growth of 1.2% for the period ended Oct. 31 and raised its full-year outlook as CEO Michael Bender said customers "have remained resilient" but are "migrating to value with their purchases.".

He tied improvement to the manufacturer's work on product assortment, store experience and value.

Best Buy also on Tuesday posted its highest comparable sales growth in five years, at 6.1%, which prompted the electronics retailer to raise its full-year outlook.

"We have a tremendous amount of momentum," CEO Jason Bonfig told CNBC in an interview. "The fact that we saw pretty much broad-based growth across almost all of our categories is a lot of momentum that we're very excited about.".

The firm also credited execution, market share gains and a compelling product cycle alongside growing customer demand.

At Dick's Sporting Goods, quarterly comparable sales rose 2.6% at the core business and 0.5% at Foot Locker. CEO Lauren Hobart said "all income demographics grew" and the company "didn't see trade-down from best to better or better to good.".

In a recent development, she similarly pointed to upcoming products and market share gains within the category as contributing to the strong quarter. She also highlighted continued improvement at Foot Locker.

All three companies have been undergoing efforts to boost sales and get the right products on shelves to meet customer demand.

Target, likewise undergoing revitalization efforts, last week reported comparable sales growth of 5.6% in the third quarter, fueled by a 5% increase in comparable traffic. The retailer raised its full-year outlook.

CEO Michael Fiddelke at the time called the traffic gain "a healthy sign that guests are responding to our changes and choosing Target more often.".

Even Gap CEO Richard Dickson told CNBC the tech giant has moved from "rebuild mode" to "turnaround mode" at its Old Navy banner, a sign of progress, albeit not a broad-based portfolio recovery.

Recent findings suggest that michael Baker, a retail analyst at D.A. Davidson, told CNBC he sees both a resilient consumer and tech giant-specific improvements as driving sector strength.

It has been revealed that "Retail sales have been more resilient than most think," Baker said. His analysis highlighted retail sales, excluding autos and gas, rose 5.1% in the third quarter on a nonseasonally adjusted basis — the strongest quarter since the pandemic.

But he cautioned that growth appears to be coming more from transaction size than traffic, with inflation, promotions and higher units per transaction driving up spend.

Industry observers note that dollar Tree, which reported better-than-expected earnings on Tuesday morning, posted a 3.8% increase to traffic, accelerating from 0.4% growth in the prior quarter, suggesting more shoppers may be bargain hunting. Comparable sales at the retailer increased 4.6% during the period.

Recent findings suggest that "Consumers are under pressure, and they are increasingly selective about where and how they spend," mentioned Dollar Tree CEO Michael Creedon on the manufacturer's earnings call. "When under pressure, shoppers prioritize value and buy closer to need.".

Comparable sales of everyday essentials rose 8.9% at Dollar Tree stores in the third quarter, while sales of nonessential items were essentially flat, the company mentioned.

— CNBC's Laya Neelakandan contributed to this report.

#219412. Britain's pound is beating every other major currency this year

📅 04 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (516 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

Britain's pound is beating every other major currency this year

📅 04 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 3 min read (516 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the British pound crashed to a record low last fall as investors rebelled against budget plans by former Prime Minister Liz Truss.
  • Sterling hit its highest level against the US dollar in 10 months on Tuesday, topping $1.25 for the first time since June 2022.
  • The UK currency has been boosted by indications the country’s economy is holding up better than expected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the British pound crashed to a record low last fall as investors rebelled against budget plans by former Prime Minister Liz Truss. Now, it’s enjoying a comeback.

Sterling hit its highest level against the US dollar in 10 months on Tuesday, topping $1.25 for the first time since June 2022. The pound, which has advanced about 3.3% versus the greenback since the start of 2023, is the best-performing currency among developed economies this year.

The UK currency has been boosted by indications the country’s economy is holding up better than expected. Activity is now thought to have expanded 0.1% in the final three months of last year, up from a previous estimate of no growth at all. Gross domestic product growth in January has been estimated at 0.3% after dropping 0.5% in December.

This resilience is bolstering expectations the Bank of England will maintain aggressive interest rate hikes despite concerns about the health of the global banking sector. Rising rates can boost the domestic currency because they help attract foreign investors searching for higher returns.

Inflation in the United Kingdom also jumped to an annual rate of 10.4% in February, underscoring the need for the Bank of England to maintain its tough approach.

The pound plunged close to $1.03 in September 2022 after the Truss government unveiled aims to boost borrowing while slashing taxes, unleashing panic in financial markets that fueled fears of a recession in the United Kingdom.

The International Monetary Fund predicted in January that the UK economy would contract by 0.6% this year, while all other advanced economies would grow, if only slightly.

“There was a lot of pessimism being priced into the pound,” said Francesco Pesole, a currency strategist at ING.

But the sharp pullback in energy prices and China’s reopening have provided some relief about the economic outlook since the start of the year.

“There was a significant re-rating of growth expectations around Europe, and that impacted the UK,” Pesole noted.

The euro has also been lifted by these dynamics, rising 2.3% against the US dollar in 2023. The pound’s rally has been sharper in large part because its 2022 declines were more severe, according to Pesole.

Both currencies have been aided by the greenback’s sharp drop from highs reached last September as recession fears have percolated in the United States.

Sources indicate that A lack of clarity around the Federal Reserve’s next steps has also restrained the dollar in recent weeks. Investor speculation has increased that the Fed could pause or stop rate hikes due to concerns about the economy following the failure of Silicon Valley Bank last month.

Jordan Rochester, a currency strategist at Nomura, noted he thinks the pound could rise to $1.30 this year and “potentially higher.” But he still sees risks given the uncertainty surrounding the Bank of England’s plans and how rate rises will feed back through the country’s economy. And Pesole cautioned that currency fluctuations are often overdone when markets are choppy, as they are now.

“In a volatile market environment, moves are exacerbated,” he mentioned.

#219409. This 345-million-year-old fossil had scientists fooled for decades

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (888 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

This 345-million-year-old fossil had scientists fooled for decades

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (888 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A small fossil discovered in Scotland and regarded for nearly three decades as one of the earliest known reptiles has turned out to be a very different kind of prehistoric animal.
  • Industry observers note that the 345-million-year-old fossil, discovered in 1984, belongs to a species called Westlothiana lizziae.
  • In a recent development, although the fossil's distorted condition made its anatomy difficult to interpret, researchers widely regarded it as the earliest known amniote adapted to life on land.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A small fossil discovered in Scotland and regarded for nearly three decades as one of the earliest known reptiles has turned out to be a very different kind of prehistoric animal. Newly introduced research published in Nature is challenging its long-established place in evolutionary history. The study was led by scientists at the American Museum of Natural History and the University of Oxford, working in collaboration with the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility.

Industry observers note that the 345-million-year-old fossil, discovered in 1984, belongs to a species called Westlothiana lizziae. Nicknamed "Lizzie" because of its resemblance to a lizard, the specimen consists of a nearly complete skeleton preserved in two crushed slabs of rock. Early descriptions relied largely on anatomical features visible at the surface, including four limbs with fingers and toes that appeared to have claw-like tips. These characteristics distinguished Westlothiana from many other animals living at the time, whose limbs more closely resembled fins.

In a recent development, although the fossil's distorted condition made its anatomy difficult to interpret, researchers widely regarded it as the earliest known amniote adapted to life on land. Amniotes are a major group of vertebrates that includes reptiles, birds, and mammals. Following its scientific description in 1990, Westlothiana became an important reference point for researchers investigating when and how these animals first evolved.

"Lizzie has been an icon for the early evolution of amniotes for decades," stated Xavier Jenkins, a postdoctoral fellow in the Museum's Division of Paleontology and co-lead author of the study. "But when we were finally able to see inside the fossil, we found an animal that looked very different from what we expected.".

Advanced X-Ray Scans Reveal Lizzie's True Identity.

Using powerful X-ray imaging technology at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility in Grenoble, France, the scientists peered beneath the surface of the rock and reconstructed previously inaccessible parts of the animal's anatomy.

What they discovered was strikingly different from the anatomy expected in an early reptile. Lizzie possessed a primitive skull, internal gills containing bone, and a mouth resembling that of a fish, complete with thousands of tiny teeth. Together, these features rule out its previously proposed position within the evolutionary lineage leading to reptiles. Instead of living primarily on land, Westlothiana appears to have been an aquatic or amphibious animal.

It has been revealed that "The surprisingly primitive features of the skull show us that Lizzie was not only not a reptile but belonged to a much more ancient lineage. It turns out looks can be deceiving, and Lizzie lived a completely different lifestyle than we previously thought," noted Ben Igielman, co-lead author of the study, who started this research during his graduate work at the University of Oxford.

Reptile-Like Features Evolved in Aquatic Ancestors.

The discovery also changes how scientists understand the origins of several anatomical features traditionally associated with vertebrates adapted to terrestrial environments.

Researchers now believe that characteristics such as claws and the arrangement of five digits on each hand and foot, a pattern familiar in reptiles and mammals, had already emerged in earlier animals that were still closely associated with water. These creatures belonged to the evolutionary lineage leading to tetrapods, the broader group of four-limbed vertebrates that encompasses both amphibians and amniotes.

"This is a substantial surprise," said study co-author Roger Benson, the Museum's Macaulay Curator of Paleontology. "It shows that, although we think of amphibians as being more 'primitive' than reptiles today, some of the traits of reptiles were already there in the ancestor of both amphibians and reptiles.".

Ancient Footprints May Tell a Different Story.

In a recent development, the findings could also have crucial implications for the interpretation of prehistoric fossil tracks. Recently discovered trackways have been used as evidence that amniotes first appeared during the Devonian Period, more than 359 million years ago.

Recent findings suggest that these ancient impressions record the movements of a four-limbed animal with apparently clawed digits. However, if distant relatives of tetrapods such as Westlothiana also possessed claws, such footprints are no longer sufficient on their own to identify the animals that left them as amniotes.

Some trackways previously attributed to early amniotes may instead have been left by more ancient, amphibious creatures belonging to the evolutionary lineage of tetrapods.

"The broader lesson is that terrestrial-looking traits, such as a reptile-like foot, a weight-bearing forelimb, and claw-like phalanges were not unique features of tetrapods, but rather accumulated piecemeal in their close relatives, in animals that were still living in and out of the water," Jenkins mentioned.

Additional contributors to the study include Jason Head from the University of Cambridge, Vincent Fernandez from the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility, Lucy Roberts from the Natural History Museum, London, and Timothy Smithson from the University Museum of Zoology Cambridge.

The research received funding from the National Science Foundation (grant number EAR-PF 2518154), the National Environment Research Council (grant numbers NE/S000739/1, NE/W007576/1, and NE/L002507/1), and the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (grant number BB/X014819/1).

Welcome to the Repair Café, Where Neighbors Fight Throwaway Culture

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1559 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story originally appeared on Grist and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
  • According to recent reports, on an unusually cool and rainy Saturday morning in Decatur, Georgia, dozens of people filed into a warehouse at the back of a church parking lot, their arms full of what a less hopeful group might call junk.
  • That’s how Lilly Pettus ended up shoulder to shoulder with three strangers, their hands all pressing together the pieces of her family’s cracked dining room chair as wood glue hardened and a volunteer tightened a clamp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story originally appeared on Grist and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

According to recent reports, on an unusually cool and rainy Saturday morning in Decatur, Georgia, dozens of people filed into a warehouse at the back of a church parking lot, their arms full of what a less hopeful group might call junk. Some carried broken lamps, glitching electronics, or cracked furniture. Others walked in with toolboxes, multimeters for testing electric currents, and cans of WD-40. Beneath extension cords dangling from the rafters, they sorted themselves into smaller groups: the volunteer electricians, tailors, luthiers, carpenters, and at least one cutler (knife sharpener), commandeering nearby worktables and passersby as needed.

That’s how Lilly Pettus ended up shoulder to shoulder with three strangers, their hands all pressing together the pieces of her family’s cracked dining room chair as wood glue hardened and a volunteer tightened a clamp.

“This is so interesting,” a giddy Pettus said, inspecting for the first time the joints, one of them broken, that held together the chair she’d owned for decades. “You never even know how furniture is put together.”.

Sources indicate that this is Decatur’s semi-regular repair café, one of a few hundred meetings like it across the United States. More Americans than ever are turning to these community gatherings to fix what they already own, resisting the influence of companies that sell everything from hiking boots to smartphones and hot water boilers and that push for replacement over repair. One consequence of this throwaway economy is an increase in greenhouse gas emissions from manufacturing that threatens to intensify climate change.

Sources indicate that yet, organizers and volunteers consider repair cafés to be more than a relatively small climate solution. As inflation rises and wages stagnate, the meetups connect people to a movement with the ambitious goal of changing the fundamentals of America’s consumer economy.

At the Decatur repair café, volunteers, wearing green shirts with “I can probably fix that” printed on the back, offered their skills free of charge as patrons observed. A young father of a toddler and squirmy baby watched as a volunteer replaced a switch on a favorite mid-century modern lamp worn out by the older child’s repeated clicking. Murmurs of excitement rippled around the building as the acrid smell of a spot welding project wafted through.

Pettus’ broken chair held in its wood her family’s story. Soon after she and her husband were married in 1996, they began a search for a dining room set. Pettus wanted the chairs to be comfortable for her entire family, but one of her brothers is nearly 7 feet tall, and another just a few inches shorter. “We are not a tiny family,” Pettus remarked. “We are a big family.”.

Pettus also thought of one of her children who’d interned at the Environmental Protection Agency and shared his concerns with Pettus about pollution and climate change. Then, after months of the broken chair cluttering the family’s house, Pettus was running Saturday morning errands when she passed the Decatur repair café. She drove the half-mile home to grab the chair and decided to give it a second chance.

“When a product breaks and you have to throw it away, it’s very lonely,” remarked Martine Postma, director of Repair Café International, a Netherlands-based network of 4,000 cafés. “ It’s easier to just go on the internet and order a new item which will come to your doorstep in 24 hours, but that’s also a very lonely, disconnected activity.”.

According to recent reports, postma, a former journalist with the demeanor of an unflappable librarian, founded her organization in 2010 after the birth of her second child magnified her fears about the planet’s future. “Markets are flooded with trash—with cheap products that we don’t need and that do not work,” Postma stated. “They break, and they contribute nothing to our well-being. They just contribute waste.”.

Repair cafés appear to be inspiring people to use their stuff longer. In 2025, they prevented nearly 2 million pounds of waste—the equivalent of more than 100 fully loaded Boeing 747 aircraft—according to Repair Café International, and reduced greenhouse gas emissions equivalent to the average consumption of about 1,000 Dutch families.

Postma, Pettus, and millions of others often smack into obstacles when they try to fix their own stuff. Broken products are increasingly difficult to repair, according to a report from the Federal Trade Commission titled “Nixing the Fix.” The report details how Americans are incentivized to “replace products before the end of their useful lives” by companies that decide to make repairs less safe, limit the availability of parts, lock software and firmware, or even “disparage” independent repair.

Recent findings suggest that in 2023, California, Colorado, Minnesota, and Latest York passed “right to repair” legislation meant to encourage repair over replacement. A year later the European Union passed a similar directive. Postma and other organizers consider the cafés a natural place for activism to push for right-to-repair measures, although Postma hopes for more sweeping changes in Europe, like a tax on raw materials. She argued it would limit emissions and bolster repair shops, even if it increases the cost of products.

In a recent development, “ I feel for the objects around me. I feel sorry for them if they’re broken,” she stated. “I want to make repairing a normal thing in everyday life once more.”.

According to Postma, repairing goods is more common in relatively poor countries where replacing them can be especially difficult and expensive. It’s in wealthy countries that repair cafés are thriving, but they’re not at all uniform. Each reflects the surrounding area and its socioeconomics.

According to recent reports, on a Sunday afternoon in the Collier Heights neighborhood of Atlanta, volunteers brought most of their own tools to the basement of a building owned by a Seventh-Day Adventist Church, setting them on white plastic folding tables atop a light pink carpet. The café looked much different from the one a 30-minute drive across the city in Decatur. The median annual household income in the mostly Black Collier Heights neighborhood is roughly $40,000 lower than in Decatur. Many people who brought items wanted them fixed less for sentimental reason, and more so they could keep using them.

According to recent reports, gale Pines walked in with a red air fryer that had stopped working after they used it to dehydrate ginger. When their oven ran, Pines remarked, it heated the entire kitchen. So, while in nursing school, they cooked many of their evening meals in the air fryer, most often chicken nuggets and fries.

Pines recently graduated but had trouble finding a job and couldn’t afford to buy a new $100 air fryer. “It’s just hard to exist,” Pines said. “I don’t really have a very substantial support network outside of my friends.”.

In a recent development, one of Pines’ housemates told them about Collier Heights’ repair café. They keep a bag of broken electronics in the garage that they’d prefer not to send to a landfill. “Being in the height of climate collapse we can’t just keep buying upcoming stuff all the time, both for the economy and for our material scarcity,” Pines remarked.

It has been revealed that when a volunteer at the Collier Heights repair café opened up the air fryer, they swiftly discovered the problem: a bad capacitor. Another volunteer had brought a replacement part, and the two of them made the fix as Pines watched, impressed, but unable to follow the relatively complex repair. Pines felt OK that they hadn’t learned how to fix the air fryer themself.

“ To just be around people that want to help other people with the skills that they have, that’s value that is really vital to me and something that I try to do as well,” Pines mentioned. “If somebody in my community has a question about their medication or something and can’t afford to go to the doctor, I’m happy to answer any questions that people have.”.

Another volunteer, Lew Lefton, said he thought that the satisfaction humans draw from making and fixing things has largely been lost, but apocalyptic threats like climate change and artificial intelligence have driven many people toward rediscovering more basic, human skills that are key to survival. People who come to a repair café have a different way to view the future, according to Lefton, especially if they learn something or volunteer themselves. “If the world ends,” he said, “at least I’ll know how to fix a motor.”.

Back in Decatur, Pettus left the repair café with a newly sturdy chair. A screw and some glue fixed the crack around the joint, but the chair still needed upholstery work. Someone Pettus met at the café, who had provided one of the sets of hands that held her chair together as the glue set, advised her on where to buy fabric. Pettus thought she might bring the chair back to the repair café for help reupholstering its seat cushion.

It has been revealed that “The beauty of it,” Pettus noted, “was that I actually was able to learn more about the chair. It was a great experience to know that—I’m not gonna say I birthed it, I of course did not—but I actually had something to do with helping to get it put back together.”.

#219402. Latest Update: AI can combine mathematical ideas on a scale beyond individual human minds. But could it produce ideas likes Einstein?

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1086 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: AI can combine mathematical ideas on a scale beyond individual human minds. But could it produce ideas likes Einstein?

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1086 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last year, I asked ChatGPT to add up my British state pension contributions.
  • A friend who teaches math wasn't surprised.
  • Fast-forward to November 2026, and a mathematician working at artificial intelligence tech giant Anthropic, Levent Alpöge, claims to have solved one of the hardest problems in mathematical history with the help of the company's chatbot, Claude.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last year, I asked ChatGPT to add up my British state pension contributions. Thankfully, I double-checked. The total was wrong by a few pounds.

A friend who teaches math wasn't surprised. Chatbots, he said, often get simple calculations wrong.

Fast-forward to November 2026, and a mathematician working at artificial intelligence tech giant Anthropic, Levent Alpöge, claims to have solved one of the hardest problems in mathematical history with the help of the company's chatbot, Claude.

That problem was the Riemann hypothesis, which concerns the distribution of prime numbers, and has baffled mathematicians since 1859.

How did AI go from stumbling over simple arithmetic to scaling such extraordinary mathematical heights?

The answer lies in how AI processes information, said Andrea Asperti, a professor in computer science at Italy's University of Bologna.

Unlike conventional calculators, early chatbots were trained to predict language, producing plausible answers without necessarily doing the math.

Ironically, they may perform millions of calculations to arrive at the wrong answer.

"In a sense, asking why a chatbot makes arithmetic mistakes despite its enormous computational power is like asking why humans make mistakes in mental arithmetic despite having billions of neurons in their brains," Asperti told DW.

Ken Ono, a mathematics professor at the University of Virginia in the United States, recalled how Google's Gemini once concluded that 9.11 was greater than 9.8.

"But make no mistake, those errors are very rare today," Ono told DW.

Asperti attributed AI's gains to gradual improvements in model size, training data and methods rather than a single breakthrough.

AI can now explore different approaches, check its work, correct mistakes and use specialized computational tools.

"What is remarkable is that these relatively incremental technological improvements have resulted in qualitative leaps in intellectual capabilities," Asperti said.

Perhaps most surprising was AI's ability to solve previously unsolved problems — something many had doubted it could do.

"Solving open mathematical problems requires a considerable degree of creativity: it is not simply a matter of retrieving existing knowledge or reproducing known arguments," Asperti said.

Kevin Buzzard, a mathematician at Imperial College London, UK, was excited but not surprised by the proposed proof of the Riemann hypothesis.

He had already seen AI resolve a problem in algebraic geometry by finding a counterexample.

"I had thought about the problem myself and could see what the difficulties were. AI cut through them," Buzzard told DW.

Ono draws an analogy with chess: While humans struggle to think several moves ahead, AI can explore countless possibilities. In advanced mathematics, the scope is far greater.

Sources indicate that "When it comes to pure mathematics, there are tens of thousands of research papers that are the individual moves that it gets to play with. And what we're seeing is the power of that capacity," Ono noted.

Another advantage is AI's ability to recognize connections across different areas of mathematics.

Recent findings suggest that "Most of us become specialists, building upon theories that we learn over time. And it's difficult to become proficient in many more than a small handful of areas," Ono said.

The proposed Riemann proof illustrates that breadth. "It might be 30 or 40 mathematicians you would have to put in a room before you could assemble this proof," he said.

And AI's knowledge extends well beyond math.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Ono suggested that the mathematician behind the Claude-assisted proof could have interrupted his work to ask the chatbot: "Hey, by the way, next week I'm going to Hawaii. Come up with a beautiful itinerary for a long weekend in Hawaii.".

He and Claude could then have seamlessly returned to advanced mathematics.

"The point I make there is that Claude seems to know everything at a fairly deep level, and humans don't," Ono said.

Ono suggests the individual ideas behind the proposed proof may all be within human intellectual reach.

"But the sheer scope and the ability to assemble ideas that had never been assembled before, that is what is extraordinary here," he noted.

Ono called the achievement "superhuman.".

Asperti believes AI could develop an entirely different kind of mathematical intuition.

Mathematicians work with abstract spaces of hundreds or thousands of dimensions, which humans, living in a three-dimensional world, struggle to visualize.

AI might develop its own ways of understanding such structures and "discover relationships that are difficult for us even to imagine," Asperti said.

Ono is excited about the future of mathematics but concerned about the future of mathematicians.

Until recently, he would have discouraged young mathematicians from tackling problems like the Riemann hypothesis, saying they could spend 20 years without producing any results.

"Shoot for the moon! The bar has been raised so high that if your primary interest as a mathematician is in the questions themselves, then this is a great time.".

"The flip side, if you're a mathematician and your identity is that you want to be the source of the ideas, well, you may have lost most of that.".

Ono, who has trained 35 PhD students, is "deeply worried" about their future.

"Make no mistake. In the year 2026, the ground shifted beneath the entire edifice of the world of human mathematical research," he noted.

Ono believes the role of future mathematicians will be "much more like being a conductor of the most extraordinary orchestra.".

In the past, mathematicians were trained by getting them to prove theorems.

"Now you can prove a theorem by pressing a button," noted Buzzard, "so we need upcoming methods.".

Buzzard is setting up a lab that emphasizes understanding, explaining and defending complex mathematical arguments.

"The best team for doing mathematics is a computer plus human team, and it is still relatively straightforward to extract insights and understanding from what machines are doing," he said.

But, he stated, mathematical research may "end up completely dominated by machines doing things which humans simply cannot comprehend any more, very cheaply and at the touch of a button.".

Industry observers note that so, that is the glitch of solving mathematical problems. What about AI's ability to come up with mathematical problems and propositions, like an Albert Einstein?

Sources indicate that ono noted: "If you trained a large language model on all the mathematics and all the physics that was known by the end of the 19th century, would a model spin up Einstein's theory of relativity on its own? I don't think we've seen that sort of creative spark, that sort of ability yet.".

#219401. Breaking: These bizarre prehistoric mammals may have been misunderstood for 150 years

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1371 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: These bizarre prehistoric mammals may have been misunderstood for 150 years

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1371 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For generations, paleontologists have regarded an extinct group of giant mammals known as uintatheres as a textbook example of sexual dimorphism, the physical differences between males and females of the same species.
  • It has been revealed that recognizable by their enormous bodies, prominent horns, and oversized canine teeth, uintatheres first appeared approximately 58 million years ago, less than 10 million years after an asteroid wiped out the dinosaurs.
  • However, fresh research from the University of Kansas published in PLOS One suggests that the physical differences between male and female uintatheres may have been considerably less pronounced than scientists have long assumed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For generations, paleontologists have regarded an extinct group of giant mammals known as uintatheres as a textbook example of sexual dimorphism, the physical differences between males and females of the same species.

It has been revealed that recognizable by their enormous bodies, prominent horns, and oversized canine teeth, uintatheres first appeared approximately 58 million years ago, less than 10 million years after an asteroid wiped out the dinosaurs. These unusual mammals persisted for roughly 20 million years.

However, fresh research from the University of Kansas published in PLOS One suggests that the physical differences between male and female uintatheres may have been considerably less pronounced than scientists have long assumed.

"Males have been interpreted as being much larger and possessing far more dramatic cranial features than females," mentioned study author Kevin Mulcahy, doctoral student at the KU Biodiversity Institute & Natural History Museum.

A Broken Fossil Tooth Leads to an Unexpected Discovery.

The investigation began when Mulcahy and his doctoral adviser, K. Christopher Beard, senior curator at the institute, attempted to identify a broken upper molar recovered during fieldwork in Montana. The researchers suspected the tooth belonged to a uintathere but needed additional fossil specimens to confirm its identity.

In a recent development, "We had a research visit at the American Museum of Natural History in Newly introduced York, where our main goal was just to compare that tooth to teeth from other uintatheres and figure out what type of animal we had," Mulcahy stated. "They have this big collection -- entire shelves occupied with these skulls, and each one of them is almost a meter long. These are famous specimens that are in the literature, and I was originally just looking at them to compare their teeth, and I noticed a ton of variation in a way that didn't appear binary.".

Intrigued by the unexpected range of physical characteristics, Mulcahy began measuring the skulls in the museum's collection.

Recent findings suggest that "I just, really hastily, with a ruler, gathered a bunch of measurements of the skulls while we were there," Mulcahy said. "I started playing around with statistics, and there are ways you can look at different measurements to see if they're best fit by a classic unimodal distribution, or if you were to think you're dealing with something that exhibits strong sexual dimorphism, you'd see something with a bimodal distribution -- that there are two means, one for males and one for females.".

Ancient Skulls Challenge a Classic Example of Sexual Dimorphism.

If males and females differed as dramatically as paleontologists had suggested, the skull measurements would be expected to cluster into two relatively distinct groups. Instead, Mulcahy's initial analysis failed to reveal such a clear separation.

"It wasn't like there's one group of specimens that look bigger than another, and then there's another group that are smaller with smaller horns and canines," he said. "So I was kind of interested -- are these really good examples of sexual dimorphism after all? Is there actual evidence in the morphology of these skulls, in the distribution in particular of the ranges of morphology we're seeing, that that's what's going on?".

Sources indicate that to investigate further, Mulcahy collected additional measurements from fossils housed at other institutions and expanded his analysis using latest statistical methods. His final dataset encompassed approximately 30 skulls belonging to a single extinct species, Uintatherium anceps.

Industry observers note that although the results offered some hints of physical differences between the sexes, the evidence was far less convincing than expected. One major challenge in studying extinct animals is that researchers generally cannot independently determine the sex of individual fossil specimens.

"Maybe there were some little signals of dimorphism here and there, but nothing really concrete," he said. "I had an idea: Maybe it's just that the techniques I'm using aren't robust enough to actually measure sexual dimorphism. With fossil animals, you don't actually know which specimens are males and which are females. You can guess and then test whether or not the ones you guess are males differ from the ones you guess are females, but that's super circular, because you could just be picking the most extreme ones to be one sex and the least extreme to be the other. Of course they're going to differ.".

Modern Bison Provide an Key Comparison.

Sources indicate that to determine whether his statistical methods could reliably detect sexual dimorphism, Mulcahy turned to a living mammal: the bison. Unlike fossil uintatheres, modern bison specimens could be classified by sex with confidence.

Bison also offered a useful comparison because they are large, horned herbivores whose ecology shares similarities with what researchers have proposed for uintatheres.

"When you're dealing with living animals, you can just take the males, take the females and compare them," he remarked. "Bison are another really big herbivore, with a similar sort of ecology that's been proposed for uintatheres, and they also have big horns. What I noticed is that the signals of dimorphism I was picking up in bison were a lot clearer. When I was looking at the bison, it was almost perfect that all of the females were most similar to the females, and all the males were most similar to the males.".

Industry observers note that the contrast suggests that the relatively weak evidence for sexual dimorphism in uintatheres cannot be attributed solely to limitations of the statistical techniques. The same methods successfully identified much clearer physical differences between male and female bison.

Victorian-Era Bias May Have Shaped Paleontology.

In a recent development, mulcahy believes that historical cultural attitudes may help explain why paleontologists came to accept such pronounced differences between male and female uintatheres. Many extinct species were first identified and described during the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when prevailing views about the sexes may have influenced scientific interpretations.

"Back then, this is right when evolutionary theory, sexual selection, natural selection, all of that is kind of coming into play," he said. "I think it's really important to remember that these things were first discovered in the late 1800s by a bunch of male paleontologists working in a very Victorian-era mindset. The idea is basically assumed at that point that males are going to be bigger and scarier than females. It's really interesting: When you step back and actually test that hypothesis, it doesn't really hold up.".

It has been revealed that because uintatheres have long been regarded as one of the clearest examples of sexual dimorphism in the fossil record, the new findings could have implications beyond these unusual prehistoric giants. Other extinct species may also have exhibited less pronounced physical differences between males and females than scientists have traditionally believed.

Rethinking the Evolution of Sex Differences in Mammals.

According to recent reports, the research also adds to a growing body of evidence challenging the widespread assumption that male mammals are typically larger than females. Dramatic differences in body size and physical appearance may have evolved independently in multiple mammalian lineages rather than being a characteristic inherited from their earliest common ancestors.

Research on living mammals has similarly challenged conventional thinking, suggesting that pronounced differences favoring larger males are less widespread than historically assumed.

"Strong, big male-style sexual dimorphism was probably not ancestral at the root of the mammalian tree, and among the mammals where we do see this pattern today, it's almost certainly shown up independently several times," Mulcahy mentioned. "It had long been assumed that sexual dimorphism is the norm, that most species show that males are bigger than females. But just a couple years ago, a paper came out showing that among living mammals, most species either don't show any dimorphism or actually have larger females. The idea that males are always bigger than females is really just a choice of what animals were people looking at, what are the things that biologists in the past were interested in.".

#219393. Latest Update: Scientists identify two ages when children may be most vulnerable to screen time

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (973 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Scientists identify two ages when children may be most vulnerable to screen time

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (973 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that screen time at certain ages may be more closely tied to children's future learning and memory than previously recognized.
  • Recent findings suggest that the findings suggest that when children use screens may be just as notable as how much time they spend in front of them.
  • In a recent development, as digital devices become an increasingly common part of childhood, understanding their potential long-term effects has become a growing priority.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that screen time at certain ages may be more closely tied to children's future learning and memory than previously recognized. A latest study tracking children from age 1 to 8 found that those who spent more time watching screens during infancy and around the start of elementary school tended to perform worse academically at age 9 and have weaker working memory at age 10.5.

Recent findings suggest that the findings suggest that when children use screens may be just as notable as how much time they spend in front of them. Two ages in particular, 1 and 6, emerged as potentially sensitive periods in childhood development.

In a recent development, as digital devices become an increasingly common part of childhood, understanding their potential long-term effects has become a growing priority. Recommendations from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the American Academy of Pediatrics generally emphasize avoiding screen exposure during the first 18 to 24 months of life and limiting it to less than one hour a day for children ages 2 to 5. However, many young children spend considerably more time using screens.

Tracking Screen Time Throughout Childhood.

Despite growing concerns about children's digital habits, previous research has produced mixed findings about the relationship between screen time and cognitive development. Many earlier studies examined children at a single point in time, concentrated on children already attending school, or did not regularly track screen habits throughout early childhood.

Following the same children over several years allows researchers to investigate whether screen exposure at particular ages is more strongly associated with later outcomes. This approach can also help researchers better account for the influence of family circumstances and environmental factors.

According to recent reports, scientists from Inserm and the National University of Singapore addressed these gaps in a study published in the World Journal of Pediatrics. The researchers examined data from 502 children participating in the Growing Up in Singapore Towards healthy Outcomes (GUSTO) birth cohort.

In a recent development, parents reported their children's screen viewing habits at six different points between infancy and middle childhood. The researchers then evaluated the children's academic achievement and working memory several years later.

Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and manipulate information. It plays an essential role in everyday learning, allowing children to follow instructions, solve math problems, understand sentences, and keep track of information while completing tasks.

Two Ages Stand Out for Screen Time Risks.

The researchers found that greater screen exposure at certain stages of childhood was associated with lower academic achievement and poorer working memory later in life. These relationships were particularly consistent among children who spent more time watching screens at age 1 and around age 6, when formal schooling typically begins.

In a recent development, children who accumulated more screen time throughout childhood also tended to achieve lower academic scores. However, the strength of the associations varied depending on when the exposure occurred, suggesting that some developmental stages may be more sensitive than others.

Recent findings suggest that one possible explanation is that screen viewing can take time away from activities that support cognitive development, including conversations with caregivers, imaginative play, and hands-on exploration of the physical world. These experiences provide opportunities for children to develop language, attention, memory, and problem-solving skills.

"The effect sizes we saw at age 1 were the largest among all time points we examined," the authors said. "That suggests early infancy may be a window of heightened sensitivity, when the developing brain is particularly vulnerable to the displacement of learning interactions by screen time. We were also surprised to see that while screen use at age 2 and 3 did not show significant links, the associations re-emerged at age 6 -- when children enter formal schooling. So it is not just about early years; screen use later in childhood still matters.".

Although the study identifies associations rather than proving that screen time directly causes poorer cognitive or academic outcomes, the results highlight the potential importance of managing children's screen habits at different ages.

Why Even Small Differences in Screen Time Matter.

According to the researchers, the results reinforce the principle that "less is better" when it comes to children's screen time.

Sources indicate that an additional hour of daily screen viewing may not produce a noticeable difference in an individual child's academic abilities. However, when similar patterns occur across a large population, even relatively small differences in average performance could increase the number of children who experience academic difficulties.

The researchers suggest that efforts to encourage healthier screen habits could begin during infancy, with renewed emphasis around the transition to elementary school. This approach recognizes that children's developmental needs continue to change well beyond their toddler years.

The authors also stress that the amount of time children spend in front of screens is only one part of a much larger picture. Future studies should investigate whether the quality of digital content, the types of devices children use, and whether parents watch and interact with their children during screen time influence developmental outcomes.

Understanding these differences could eventually help researchers develop more targeted recommendations that consider not only how much screen time children get, but also when and how they engage with digital technology.

Sources indicate that the GUSTO study was supported by the Singapore National Research Foundation and the Singapore Ministry of Health's National Medical Research Council (NMRC/TCR/004-NUS/2008 and NMRC/TCR/012-NUHS/2014). Additional funding came from the Agence Nationale de la Recherche (ANR) in France (iSCAN project, ANR-20-CE36-0001).
